title: LLM evals that catch regressions before users do
excerpt: Benchmark scores do not tell you if Tuesday's prompt change broke your checkout flow. Here is the eval setup I use to catch real regressions in production features.
content:
Teams ship LLM changes the same way they used to ship CSS: tweak, eyeball one example, deploy. Then someone notices the assistant started refusing valid requests, or worse — approving invalid ones.

The fix is not "run MMLU again." It is a regression suite tied to your actual product behavior.

---

## Start from production failures, not leaderboard tasks

Every support escalation and every thumbs-down is a free test case. I export:

- User input (redacted)
- Model output
- Expected behavior label: pass / fail / ambiguous
- Feature version and prompt hash

Fifty high-quality real failures beat five hundred synthetic happy-path prompts.

---

## Three eval layers

### Layer 1 — Deterministic checks (fast, cheap)

Run on every PR:

- JSON schema validation for structured outputs
- Regex or allowlist checks on tool names and URLs
- Max length, banned phrases, PII patterns
- Latency and token budget ceilings

These catch the dumb breaks instantly.

### Layer 2 — Golden behavior set (medium cost)

Human-labeled cases for core flows:

- "Should answer from docs" — verify citation present
- "Should refuse policy violation" — verify safe refusal
- "Should call tool X" — verify exact tool + args shape

Score with rule-based graders first. Use an LLM-as-judge only when rules cannot express the criterion — and keep a human audit sample weekly.

### Layer 3 — Red team set (nightly)

Prompt injection, jailbreaks, tool misuse attempts, data exfil strings. Track pass rate over time. A drop here blocks promote even if happy-path accuracy looks fine.

---

## Example CI gate

```yaml
- name: Run LLM regression evals
  run: |
    python evals/run.py \
      --suite golden \
      --min-pass-rate 0.95 \
      --max-latency-p95 2500
```

If `golden` drops below 95% or p95 latency regresses more than 10% from baseline, the deploy stops. No manual override without a named owner.

---

## Track versions, not vibes

Store with every eval run:

- `prompt_version` or git SHA of prompt files
- Model name + temperature
- Retrieval index version (for RAG)
- Tool schema version

When a regression appears, you need to diff configurations — not guess which deploy caused it.

---

## Production sampling closes the loop

CI cannot cover the long tail. Sample 1–5% of live traffic into offline eval weekly:

- Re-run updated graders on recent production outputs
- Flag drift in refusal rate, tool error rate, citation rate
- Auto-open tickets when metrics move more than 2σ from a 14-day baseline

---

## What I stopped doing

- Chasing single-number accuracy on synthetic data
- Letting "looks fine in the playground" count as a test plan
- Running evals only after a user complaint

---

## Minimum viable eval stack

1. Export 30 real failures from prod/support.
2. Add 10 red-team cases you are afraid of.
3. Wire deterministic graders into CI.
4. Block deploy on regression.
5. Review one dashboard weekly: pass rate, latency, refusal rate.

Evals are not bureaucracy. They are how you keep prompt changes from being roulette.
